fine: Enough clothes for the weather, work and a few occasions, worn until they wear out.
excess: New outfits for every event or trend, and clothes that sit unworn.

figures.label: of water to make one T-shirt
new pieces of clothing bought worldwide each year

why.text: Clothing production almost doubled in 15 years. Textile dyeing and finishing cause 20% of global water pollution, and washing synthetic clothes puts 0.5 million tonnes of microplastics into the oceans each year.
Cotton needs large amounts of water and pesticides, polyester is made from oil, and untreated dye wastewater releases heavy metals near factories.
About half (51%) of India's textile waste is clothes and fabric thrown out by Indian consumers.

instead: Wear what you already have, and re-wear outfits at events.
Repair, alter or pass on clothes instead of throwing them away.
Swap, borrow or buy second-hand for one-off occasions.
Before buying, ask: will I wear this at least 30 times?

estimate.household: About 54,000 litres for a family of four
estimate.society: About 1.35 billion litres if 1 lakh people do it
estimate.method: 5 T-shirts × 2,700 litres of water each (Fashion and Textiles, 2023). Water used to make clothes, not tap water at home.

habit: Replacing a working phone every two or three years
fine: One phone, used until it can no longer be repaired.
excess: Upgrading because a new model is out, while the old one still works.

figures.label: of a phone's lifetime CO₂ comes from mining materials and manufacturing
of India's e-waste in 2023-24 was not processed

why.text: Because most of a smartphone's footprint comes from making it, using it longer is the best way to reduce that footprint. Most studies assume phones are used for only about 2 years.
Phone replacement cycles have become shorter than two years on average. The most common problem is the battery (42% of reported problems), which can often be replaced.
India's e-waste grew from 1.01 million tonnes in 2019-20 to 1.751 million tonnes in 2023-24.

instead: Keep your phone until it truly stops working.
Replace the battery or screen at a repair shop instead of buying new.
Buy refurbished, and use a cover and screen guard.
Give old devices to an authorised e-waste recycler, not the dustbin.

estimate.change: Keep your phone 4 years instead of 2
estimate.household: 8 fewer phones over 8 years for a family of four
estimate.society: 25,000 fewer new phones a year among 1 lakh people
estimate.method: Simple arithmetic on replacement cycles. Because about 74% of a phone's lifetime CO₂ comes from making it, each phone not made avoids most of its footprint.

habit: Eating meat and dairy every day
fine: Enough nutritious food for every meal.
excess: High-footprint animal foods at most meals, when plant foods would do.

figures.label: of greenhouse gases to produce 1 kg of beef, against 1 kg for peas
of global greenhouse gas emissions come from food
of greenhouse gases per kg of poultry meat, against 1.8 kg for pulses

why.text: Animal foods tend to have a higher footprint than plant foods: lamb and cheese both emit more than 20 kg of CO₂-equivalent per kg.
Half the world's habitable land is used for farming, and agriculture uses 70% of global freshwater withdrawals.
What you eat matters far more than how far it travelled: transport is under 10% of the footprint for most foods.

instead: Make dal, beans, chana, rajma and vegetables the centre of most meals.
Try plant-based milk, curd or paneer alternatives some days.
Eat seasonal food, but focus first on what you eat, not how far it came.

estimate.change: Swap 250 g of chicken a week for dal or other pulses
estimate.household: About 420 kg CO₂e a year for a family of four
estimate.society: About 10,500 tonnes CO₂e a year if 1 lakh people do it
estimate.method: (9.87 − 1.79 kg CO₂e per kg) × 0.25 kg × 52 weeks, using global averages from Poore and Nemecek (2018) via Our World in Data.

habit: Cooking or ordering more food than we eat
fine: Cooking what the household will eat, with a little to spare.
excess: Food that goes off in the fridge or into the bin.

figures.label: of global greenhouse gas emissions come from food that is lost or wasted

why.text: Food waste causes about a quarter of the greenhouse gas emissions from food.

instead: Plan meals and shop with a list.
Cook smaller amounts, and use leftovers for the next meal.
Share extra food with neighbours, workers or food banks.
Compost what can't be eaten.

habit: Ordering food delivery out of habit
fine: An occasional order, or when cooking is not possible.
excess: Daily orders when food is available at home, each with its own plastic and cutlery.

why.text: Food delivery adds packaging waste and carbon emissions. When one Chinese platform let customers skip cutlery, 1.1 billion orders went without it and saved 58,000 tonnes of CO₂.
Studies in Kochi and Ahmedabad found that frequent delivery use was linked to preferring unhealthy food, larger portions and noticeable changes in body weight among working professionals.

instead: Cook simple meals at home, or carry a tiffin.
When you do order, tick 'no cutlery' and choose places near you.
Eat at the restaurant, or pick up in your own container.

habit: Running the AC very cold, or in empty rooms
fine: Cooling to stay safe and sleep in extreme heat.
excess: Very low temperature settings, and AC running when nobody is in the room.

figures.label: less household electricity in India by setting the AC warmer and using fans
of extra CO₂ a year in India by 2050 from more AC, with today's power mix
of CO₂ per kWh of electricity in India in 2025

why.text: With strong warming, AC use in India could grow fourfold by 2050, adding 168 TWh of electricity demand a year, about 15% of today's use.
Use is very unequal: the richest homes use 178 kWh more electricity per person each year for AC than homes without cooling, and middle-income homes use 56% less than that.

instead: Set the AC to 24–26°C and run a fan with it.
Switch off the AC, lights and fans when you leave the room.
Use curtains, shade and cross-ventilation to keep rooms cool.
When buying, choose a high star-rated model.

estimate.change: Set the AC warmer and use a fan, in a home that cools a lot
estimate.household: About 240–290 kg CO₂ a year for a family of four
estimate.society: About 6,000–7,200 tonnes CO₂ a year if 1 lakh people do it
estimate.method: 50–60% of the 178 kWh per person per year that the highest-income homes use for AC (89–107 kWh), × 0.67 kg CO₂ per kWh for India's grid in 2025.

habit: Driving or riding alone for short trips
fine: A vehicle when there is no safe walking, cycling or public transport option.
excess: Taking the car or bike for a short trip that is easy to walk or cycle.

figures.label: less travel emissions by cycling instead of driving for short trips
less by taking a train instead of a car over medium distances
of CO₂e per km by motorbike, and 170 g by petrol car (UK factors)

why.text: Over short and medium distances, walking or cycling is nearly always the lowest-carbon way to travel. Cycling emits about 16 to 50 g of CO₂-equivalent per km, depending on how you cycle and what you eat. These are UK figures, but the ranking of modes is likely similar elsewhere.
If you must drive, sharing the car massively reduces each person's footprint, and also cuts air pollution and traffic.

instead: Walk or cycle for trips under 2–3 km.
Use the bus, metro or train for longer trips.
Share rides with colleagues or neighbours.

estimate.change: Walk or cycle a 5 km commute instead of riding a motorbike
estimate.household: About 570 kg CO₂e a year if two people in the home do it
estimate.society: About 28,500 tonnes CO₂e a year if 1 lakh people do it
estimate.method: 10 km a day × 250 working days × 0.114 kg CO₂e per km for a motorbike (UK factors via Our World in Data). Indian bikes may differ.

habit: Flying when a train will do
fine: Flying for long distances or emergencies.
excess: Short domestic flights on routes with a good train.

figures.label: less emissions by taking a train instead of a domestic flight
of CO₂e per passenger-km for a domestic flight, against 35 g by train (UK factors)

why.text: Domestic flights emit more CO₂ per passenger-km than long-haul flights, and for domestic travel even driving alone is usually better than flying.

instead: Take the train for journeys you can do overnight or in a day.
Combine trips, and use video calls for meetings.

estimate.change: Take the train for one 1,000 km trip instead of flying
estimate.person: About 210 kg CO₂e saved per one-way trip
estimate.household: About 840 kg CO₂e for a family of four
estimate.society: About 21,000 tonnes CO₂e if 1 lakh people do it once
estimate.method: 1,000 km × (0.246 − 0.035 kg CO₂e per km), UK factors via Our World in Data. Indian trains and planes may differ.

habit: Letting taps run and using more water than we need
fine: Enough clean water to drink, cook, bathe and keep the home clean.
excess: Taps left running while brushing or washing, long showers, and hosing cars or floors.

figures.label: of India's drinking and household water comes from groundwater

why.text: In 2024, 751 of India's groundwater assessment units (11.13%) were over-exploited, drawing more water than is recharged.
Water is unequal: in a Mumbai slum of 12,000 people, the price of water was the factor most strongly linked to households using 20 litres or less per person a day.

instead: Turn off the tap while brushing, shaving or soaping.
Use a bucket instead of a long shower or a hose.
Fix leaking taps and toilets quickly.
Reuse water from washing vegetables or RO waste for plants and mopping.

habit: Buying more beauty and grooming products than we use
fine: A few products you actually use up, such as soap, toothpaste and sunscreen.
excess: Shelves of half-used creams, scrubs, wipes and perfumes bought on impulse or for trends.

figures.label: of personal care products contain micro- or nanoplastics
figures.source: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (2025)

why.text: Shower gels, face cleansers and toothpaste can contain plastic microbeads, and flushing wipes down toilets also adds microplastics to wastewater.
Micro- and nanoplastics have been found in the womb, absorbed through skin, and in the lungs and gut. Global plastic production is over 450 million tonnes a year and is projected to triple by 2060.
why.source: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (2025)

instead: Finish what you have before buying more.
Choose simple products, bar soaps and refills with less packaging.
Avoid scrubs with plastic beads and never flush wipes.

habit: Buying new jewellery and accessories for every occasion
fine: A few pieces you treasure and wear for years, or pass down.
excess: New gold, watches and accessories for each event, mostly kept in a drawer.

figures.label: of global mercury emissions come from small-scale gold mining

why.text: Small-scale gold mining, which produces about 15 to 25% of the world's gold, is the largest source of mercury pollution on Earth. It releases more than 1,000 tonnes of mercury a year.
10 to 15 million people in 70 countries work in this trade, including children. Mercury exposure can damage the brain, memory and mood.

instead: Re-wear, remake or exchange old jewellery instead of buying new.
Borrow or rent accessories for one-off events.
If you buy gold, choose recycled gold where you can.

habit: Ordering small items online, one parcel at a time
fine: Buying online what you can't easily find nearby.
excess: Many small orders, each wrapped in layers that go straight into the bin.

figures.label: different packaging materials can be used for a single parcel

why.text: In an Indian survey of 285 people, orders per month rose after the pandemic, and most households threw packaging out with household waste instead of reusing or recycling it.
Mixed e-commerce packaging waste produces about 2,706 kg of CO₂-equivalent per tonne.

instead: Buy from local shops when you can, and carry your own bag.
Combine orders into one delivery, and choose minimal packaging where offered.
Reuse boxes and give clean packaging to waste pickers or recyclers.
